en.title: Yiyun Li's 'Music Against the Night' Explores Art's Immortality
en.summary: Yiyun Li's ambitious new novel, 'Music Against the Night,' plunges into the lives of two ambitious musicians. It interrogates the true cost of artistic legacy against the backdrop of historical upheaval.
en.body:
What does it truly cost to live a life in pursuit of artistic immortality? This is the profound question at the heart of **Yiyun Li**’s latest novel, **Music Against the Night**. Published by Farrar, Straus and Giroux on October 13, 2026, this magisterial work is the first in Li's much-anticipated Nocturne Trilogy. It follows the intertwined journeys of two prodigious musicians as they navigate their burgeoning careers, personal sacrifices, and the tumultuous historical shifts of the late 18th and early 19th centuries.

Li, renowned for her precise prose and unflinching exploration of human relationships, delves into the lives of these two aspiring artists, who are destined to become husband and wife. Their story unfolds against a vibrant backdrop of political and artistic change, populated by rival prodigies, irate tutors, and the true masters of their craft. The novel masterfully examines the often-fraught gulf between mere talent and genuine genius, challenging readers to consider what endures when the applause fades and history moves on.

## The Enduring Power of Art

Philip Hensher’s assertion in *A History of the Novel in Britain* that historical novels often face obsolescence resonates deeply with the themes **Music Against the Night** explores. While Hensher suggests that contemporary pleasures should outweigh concerns of posterity, Li’s novel suggests a more complex relationship between the artist, their work, and the passage of time. The pursuit of a lasting legacy, the hope that one's creations will echo through eternity, is a powerful, often consuming, ambition. **Music Against the Night** doesn't shy away from the personal toll this pursuit can exact, examining how historical upheavals can shape, challenge, and even threaten the very achievements artists strive to make immortal.

## What Fans Are Saying

Fans of **Yiyun Li** eagerly anticipate her return to fiction, particularly with a novel that promises her signature blend of intricate character studies and sweeping historical scope. The prospect of a trilogy suggests an even deeper immersion into the lives and aspirations of these musicians. The novel’s exploration of ambition, sacrifice, and the enduring impact of art speaks directly to readers who are passionate about the creative process and the legacies artists leave behind. The intricate tapestry of rivalries, mentorships, and romantic entanglements woven through the narrative is expected to captivate avid readers and newcomers alike.

## What's Next

**Music Against the Night** is now available, marking the beginning of **Yiyun Li**'s Nocturne Trilogy. Readers can look forward to further installments that will undoubtedly continue to explore the profound interplay between art, ambition, and the relentless march of history.

content_raw: What does it cost, to live your life in the hope of immortality? Li examines the gulf between talent and genius through the marriage of two real-life musicians In his recently published A History of the Novel in Britain , Philip Hensher makes a bold claim. Historical novels, he tells us, don’t last. However popular and prestigious a historical novel might be in its day, it will almost always get thrown overboard as the ship of literary culture sails on, piled high with novels of contemporary life. He might be on to something. Who now prefers Walter Scott to Jane Austen? The historical novel risks a double obsolescence, courting a future in which it has become an old-fashioned vision of an old-fashioned time. However much this news might dismay writers of historical novels, Hensher is untroubled: “As readers enjoying our contemporaries, we should not let our readerly pleasures be affected by the probability of ultimate oblivion.” Will the future, what there is of it, rate Wolf Hall as highly as we do? It doesn’t matter. Posterity, as Gore Vidal once wrote, is “a permanent darkness where no whistle sounds”. What matters is us, now, what we make of history and of our lives – in our novels and elsewhere. Continue reading...
